title: SYSK Gets Weird Playlist: The Mystery of the Mary Celeste
summary: Chuck and Josh tell the story of the Mary Celeste, the American brigantine found drifting and abandoned in the Atlantic in late November 1872 near the Azores. The episode covers the ship's unlucky history under its original name Amazon, its 1872 voyage under Captain Benjamin Spooner Briggs with his wife and two-year-old daughter, the discovery by the crew of the Dei Gratia led by Captain David Morehouse, the salvage claim at Gibraltar and the suspicious Queen's Proctor Frederick Solly Flood, the later insurance-fraud wreck near Haiti under Captain Gilman Perkins, Arthur Conan Doyle's fictional account J. Habakkuk Jephson's Statement, the list of theories (natural, murder, piracy, fraud, paranormal), and the favored explanation that the crew fled in a lifeboat fearing an explosion of denatured alcohol. The episode is part of the Gets Weird playlist and is introduced by Chuck. It also includes an unrelated listener mail segment near the end.

segments.title: Gets Weird playlist intro
segments.summary: Chuck introduces episode 5 of the Gets Weird playlist on the Mary Celeste.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts trade casual banter about New Year, orchids, miniature things, and a documentary, then introduce the Mary Celeste as a favorite mystery.

segments.title: Setting up the ghost ship story
segments.summary: Chuck recalls learning about the Mary Celeste as a child from Time Life books; Josh frames the episode and they agree on the question of what happened.

segments.title: Dinner in New York, November 1872
segments.summary: The hosts describe the November 4, 1872 dinner at the Astor House in New York with Captains Morehouse and Briggs, who were both about to sail for the Mediterranean.

segments.title: Early cursed history of the Amazon
segments.summary: The ship, originally named Amazon and built in Nova Scotia in 1860, had a fatal first captain, Robert McClellan, who died of pneumonia after a maiden voyage was aborted; the second captain, John Nutting Parker, sank another ship in the English Channel.

segments.title: Ownership changes and abandonment
segments.summary: After a storm ran the ship aground in 1867 and owners abandoned her, she was sold several times, including to Alexander McBean and Richard Haynes, for about $1,750.

segments.title: Refit and Briggs's investment
segments.summary: James Winchester's group bought and lengthened the ship; Briggs invested in a two-fifths stake and chose to captain her, bringing his wife and daughter on the maiden voyage under the new name Mary Celeste.

segments.title: Crew and departure
segments.summary: Briggs brought his wife Sarah and daughter Sophia Matilda, leaving son Arthur behind; he picked a carefully vetted seven-man crew. The ship carried 1,701 barrels of denatured alcohol and set sail November 7, 1872 for Genoa.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: The hosts announce a break before the voyage details.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-roll ad break.

segments.title: Voyage and the Azores navigation error
segments.summary: The investigation found the voyage was unremarkable until the last five days, when Briggs, miscalculating with a faulty chronometer, expected to see the Azores, changed course north, and the crew sighted land on November 25.

segments.title: Dei Gratia discovers the ship
segments.summary: Captain Morehouse's Dei Gratia spotted the Mary Celeste about 400 miles away from its logged position; first mate Oliver DeVoe and second mate John Wright boarded and found no one aboard.

segments.title: Condition of the ship and salvage value
segments.summary: The ship was found with food, water, belongings, and cargo intact, with about three and a half feet of water in the hold, a sounding rod, a disassembled pump, and partly furled sails. Salvage rights and insurer rewards made salvage valuable.

segments.title: Sailing to Gibraltar and the salvage court
segments.summary: DeVoe sailed the Mary Celeste with two other men to Gibraltar; the claim was heard before Queen's Proctor Frederick Solly Flood, who grew suspicious.

segments.title: Suspicion, investigation, and reward
segments.summary: Flood alleged foul play based on hatchet marks and supposed blood on Briggs's sword, which were found to be construction marks and rust; the court awarded a reduced reward of 1,700 pounds.

segments.title: Return to service and Haiti wreck
segments.summary: The ship returned to commerce under new owners, and was later deliberately run aground off Haiti in 1885 by Captain Gilman Perkins in an insurance fraud scheme.

segments.title: Insurance fraud scheme and barratry trial
segments.summary: Perkins claimed valuable cargo, but a salvager found junk bottles, dog collars, galoshes and rank butter; Perkins was tracked to Boston and narrowly avoided execution for barratry, with a 7-5 jury, and the law was later changed.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-roll ad break.

segments.title: Conan Doyle's fictional account
segments.summary: Arthur Conan Doyle's 1884 story J. Habakkuk Jephson's Statement in Cornhill Magazine presented sensational fabricated details, such as hot tea and a burning cigar, that were taken as fact.

segments.title: Theories: natural, murder, piracy, fraud
segments.summary: The hosts survey theories including sea quakes, waterspouts, rogue waves, sea monsters, murder by a revenge seaman or Briggs's mania, alcohol-driven mutiny, pirates, and fraud, and dismiss most based on the lack of violence and on the presence of the son Arthur.

segments.title: Paranormal theories dismissed
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck dismiss Bermuda Triangle and alien explanations.

segments.title: Evidence and the leading explanation
segments.summary: Facts including the three sails, missing lifeboat, dangling rope, and nine leaking red oak casks support the likeliest explanation: the crew abandoned ship in the lifeboat fearing an alcohol vapor explosion.

segments.title: 2006 explosion study and the lost lifeboat
segments.summary: A 2006 University College London study using butane simulated a flash explosion without soot, and the hosts describe the crew's lifeboat tethered by a long halyard that snapped, leaving them adrift.

segments.title: Listener mail from Sally
segments.summary: A listener named Sally, an Emory University sophomore who discovered the show on an exchange in Beijing, writes in praising the show.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank the listener and give contact and website information.
